content: The document titled Surveillance Guide for Vaccine-Preventable Diseases in the WHO South-East Asia Region (September 2023) focuses on invasive bacterial vaccine-preventable diseases (IB-VPDs). These diseases are caused by bacteria that invade sterile areas of the body, such as the bloodstream, soft tissues, and meninges. The primary pathogens responsible for severe invasive infections in children over one month of age include Neisseria meningitidis (meningococcus), Streptococcus pneumoniae (pneumococcus), Haemophilus influenzae, and Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B Streptococcus or GBS). These bacteria account for over half of global deaths from meningitis. While meningitis affects all age groups, newborns are particularly vulnerable to GBS, young children are at high risk for meningococcus, pneumococcus, and H. influenzae, adolescents and young adults are more susceptible to meningococcal disease, and the elderly are at increased risk for pneumococcal disease. The surveillance of IB-VPDs is a critical component of the global initiative to Defeat Meningitis by 2030. Since 2009, the World Health Organization (WHO) has coordinated a global IB-VPD surveillance network to standardize the monitoring of disease burden and etiology. The objectives of IB-VPD surveillance include quantifying disease burden and epidemiology, evaluating vaccine impact, identifying circulating serotypes or serogroups to guide vaccine selection, detecting gaps in immunization programs, monitoring antimicrobial resistance (AMR), and rapidly identifying and responding to cases, clusters, and outbreaks. Effective IB-VPD surveillance requires skilled health staff to perform procedures such as lumbar punctures and blood collection while minimizing specimen contamination. Sentinel sites should be chosen based on their ability to attract a large number of patients with the target diseases. Surveillance is not pathogen-specific and includes N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, and GBS. Laboratory capacity is essential for identifying these organisms. Surveillance can be nationwide or regional and is typically aggregate passive surveillance. In the event of a meningitis outbreak caused by N. meningitidis, a rapid public health response, including reactive vaccination, is warranted. Mass gatherings are recognized as potential settings for meningococcal disease outbreaks, and such cases must be reported under International Health Regulations (IHR). GBS surveillance requires special attention, as it is virtually nonexistent in many countries. Quantifying the burden of neonatal GBS disease is challenging, even in high-income countries, and is further complicated in lowand middle-income countries due to factors such as births outside hospital settings, early discharge of facility-born infants, limited early-life care-seeking, and lack of access to diagnostic tests and laboratory resources. Consequently, GBS disease, particularly early-onset disease occurring within the first 24–48 hours of life, is likely underrepresented in studies from these settings. The most appropriate surveillance method should be selected based on the context, and multiple methods may be required. Serosurveys and carriage studies are not recommended for routine surveillance and should be limited to research activities. The surveillance system's ability to detect and report all IB-VPDs should be evaluated through capture-recapture studies. Suspected cases of IB-VPDs should be investigated by designated surveillance officers, and case investigation forms should be completed for all suspected cases. Each case should be assigned a unique identification number (UID) that includes geographical location, year, and case number. Specimens, such as cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), blood, and pleural fluid, should be collected promptly, preferably before the administration of antibiotics, to maximize pathogen detection. However, treatment should not be delayed while awaiting laboratory results. CSF specimens should be collected via lumbar puncture and divided into three test tubes for chemical analysis, microbiological testing, and overall appearance assessment. If only one tube is available, it should be prioritized for microbiological testing. Specimens should be transported to the laboratory immediately and processed within two hours of collection. Blood specimens should be inoculated into blood culture bottles within one minute of collection and transported to the laboratory as soon as possible. Pleural fluid specimens should also be inoculated into blood culture bottles immediately and transported promptly. Specimens should be stored at room temperature and not refrigerated. Long-term storage of isolates should ideally be at -70°C, or at -20°C if further testing is required. Laboratory testing is essential for confirming IB-VPDs. CSF samples should be cultured on blood agar and chocolate agar plates, with subculturing of negative cultures after five days of incubation. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is recommended for all suspected cases, especially if antibiotics have already been administered. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), such as latex agglutination testing (LAT) and the BinaxNOW kit, can provide quick results and are useful for clinical care and outbreak identification. Gram staining is a reliable and cost-effective method for identifying pathogens if performed by well-trained staff using high-quality reagents. Strain characterization, including serogrouping and whole genome sequencing (WGS), should be performed on confirmed cases to guide vaccination efforts and understand local epidemiology. Specimens or isolates from confirmed or probable cases should be stored for further analysis. Antimicrobial resistance testing should be conducted to monitor emerging resistance and guide treatment choices. National and regional reference laboratories, as well as WHO collaborating centers, can support gene characterization and AMR testing. The Global Invasive Bacterial Vaccine-Preventable Diseases Laboratory Network, coordinated by WHO and Public Health England, supports IB-VPD surveillance through standardized laboratory procedures, data collection guidelines, and quality assurance systems.
